summary:
No measure, incident or institution specific to Mardin concerning transgender visitors is recorded in this edition's sources. Mardin province stands under the national framework of Türkiye, and no local authority in the province is documented adding bans, checkpoints or enforcement programmes of its own. What a trans visitor to Mardin faces is that national framework as it is applied by police, prosecutors and hospitals across the country.

The most consequential legal threat is pending rather than settled. Human Rights Watch reported on 29 October 2025 that a leaked omnibus, the 11th Judicial Package, would amend penal-code article 225 so that acts 'contrary to biological sex and general morality' carry up to 3 years' imprisonment and same-sex engagement or marriage ceremonies up to 4 years. The same package would amend civil-code article 40 ('Changing Sex') to raise the minimum age for gender-affirming care from 18 to 25, with mandatory infertility requirements and evaluation at a government-approved hospital, and would imprison care providers for up to 7 years and trans patients for up to 3 years. The package is national in scope and would apply in Mardin. Whether it has since passed is unresolved in the sources.

Three draft law packages targeting LGBTI people were made public during 2025, criminalising expression of LGBTI identities and consensual same-sex relations and making legal gender recognition nearly impossible, but were ultimately not submitted to parliament, according to Amnesty International's Report 2025/26. A February 2026 press report described separate legislation considering criminalising public advocacy of 'behaviour contrary to biological sex' with one to three years in prison; that provision was not included in the 2026 omnibus, the 12th judicial package.

Legal gender recognition remains formally available: transgender people in Türkiye have been able to change their legal gender since 1988, and homosexuality has not been a criminal offence since the Ottoman penal code of 1858. Marriage eligibility turns on the gender recorded in the civil registry, so a trans person who has legally changed their registered gender may marry a partner of the opposite registered gender. Same-sex marriage and civil unions are not recognised. No comprehensive law prohibits discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity.

Access to gender-affirming care is restricted. In June 2025 Türkiye's health ministry medicines agency banned prescription and supply of hormones for gender-affirming procedures for people under 21, despite existing law permitting access from 18. Hormone replacement therapy is not covered by the government healthcare system, so trans visitors must obtain and pay for it privately.

Public assembly carries documented risk. In June 2025 authorities issued blanket bans against the Istanbul LGBTI and trans pride marches; police subjected peaceful protesters to unlawful use of force, over 90 people were arbitrarily detained, three activists were remanded in prison on 29 June and released on 8 August pending trial, and prosecutions of 92 people for participating in pride marches continued at year's end. Since 2015 authorities have banned pride events in most years, using tear gas, water cannon and mass detentions against those who defied the bans. In December 2025 an İzmir court ordered the dissolution of the Young LGBTI+ Association for sharing 'obscene' images incompatible with 'society's moral values'.

In September 2026 coordinated raids under the 'My Family is Safe' crackdown involved 162 suspects, 9 associations and 13 businesses. Openly LGBTQ people are barred from the military. In ILGA-Europe's 2026 Rainbow ranking Türkiye placed 47th of 49.
tangentialFactors:
Mardin's position in southeastern Türkiye places it within the national legal and policing framework described above, but the sources record no Mardin-specific enforcement action, local ordinance or provincial initiative concerning transgender people. The province's distance from Istanbul, Ankara and İzmir means the documented pride-ban enforcement, street stops and prison deaths are concentrated elsewhere; this is a gap in the sources, not evidence of a different local practice.

The pending 11th Judicial Package and the three unpublished 2025 draft packages would, if enacted, apply uniformly across Türkiye including Mardin. The February 2026 report on criminalising public advocacy of 'behaviour contrary to biological sex' and the September 2026 'My Family is Safe' raids indicate continuing legislative and policing attention to LGBTI people through 2026, though whether any of these measures now bind in Mardin is unresolved in the sources.
localsOnly:
Trans residents of Mardin province live under the national framework: legal gender change has been available since 1988, but no comprehensive anti-discrimination law covers sexual orientation or gender identity, and the June 2025 health-ministry ban on hormone prescription and supply for under-21s applies to them alongside the exclusion of hormone replacement therapy from government healthcare coverage.

Local LGBTI associations and venues in Mardin are exposed to the pattern documented elsewhere in Türkiye: in September 2026 coordinated raids under the 'My Family is Safe' crackdown involved 162 suspects, 9 associations and 13 businesses nationwide, and in December 2025 an İzmir court dissolved an LGBTI+ association over 'obscene' material. Whether Mardin-based organisations were among those targeted is not recorded in these sources.

Whether the 11th Judicial Package has been enacted, and whether the three unpublished 2025 draft packages or the February 2026 proposal on public advocacy have since been submitted, is unresolved in the sources.

No Mardin-specific incident, arrest, local ordinance, hospital practice or police directive concerning transgender visitors or residents appears in this edition's inventory; the absence of such records is not sourced evidence that none exists.

The sources do not state whether Mardin's own police, hospitals or municipality have implemented or diverged from the national practices described, nor whether any local LGBTI organisation operates in the province.
